summaries.example: Imagine drawing a triangle on a very large, curved map. In Euclid’s geometry, its three corner angles add up to two right angles. In Lobachevskian geometry, they add up to less than that. This shows that changing one starting rule can create a whole different kind of geometry.
summaries.summary: Nineteenth-century geometry changed from a mainly Euclidean subject into a large family of theories about space. Lobachevsky and Bolyai showed that Euclid’s parallel postulate could be rejected while building a new, consistent-looking geometry. Projective geometry added special “ideal” points so that projection rules would have fewer exceptions. Felix Klein proposed understanding each geometry through its transformations and its invariants, meaning the features that those transformations preserve. Mathematicians also made geometry more strictly axiomatic: instead of trusting diagrams or the familiar meanings of words, they listed basic ideas and rules and demanded complete proofs. Riemann widened geometry again by allowing spaces whose curvature could vary. His work helped prepare mathematics for descriptions of physical space that need not be Euclidean. Lie groups gave a way to study smooth changes, including rotations, and became important in later physics. These developments also changed philosophy. Euclidean geometry no longer looked like the only possible model of certain knowledge or the only possible shape of physical space.
key_ideas: In the 1800s, geometry grew into several different kinds of geometry.
Mathematicians learned that Euclid’s fifth postulate was not the only possible choice.
Projective geometry studies features of shapes that remain after projecting them, such as onto another surface.
Klein organized geometries by looking at transformations and what those transformations leave unchanged.
Riemann developed a wider way to describe curved spaces, and Lie groups later connected geometry with smooth changes such as rotations.
summaries.why_it_matters: This story teaches that mathematics can grow by examining its own starting rules. It also shows that a theory can be useful without matching ordinary pictures exactly. Different geometries became tools for asking different questions about space, movement, and the physical world. Their success made philosophers reconsider how mathematical certainty and scientific knowledge work.

important_terms.definition: A starting rule accepted so that other geometric statements can be proved from it.
A system of ideas and rules used to study shapes, space, or distance.
A geometry in which Euclid’s rule about parallel lines is not used and triangle angles add up to less than two right angles.
A statement proved by using definitions and starting rules.
A feature that stays the same when something is changed in an allowed way.

questions_to_think_about: Can a different starting rule lead to a different but logically useful world of geometry?
Why might a picture help us understand geometry but not be enough to prove something?
What features of a shape stay the same when the shape is moved or projected?
How could geometry help scientists describe the physical world?

summaries.example: Consider a disk bounded by a conic. Klein showed that, inside this region, a distance can be constructed from a projective quantity called the cross-ratio. With the right conic and transformations, that distance behaves like Lobachevskian distance. Thus a geometry that appears to be about projective figures can contain the theorems of a non-Euclidean metric geometry.
summaries.summary: The entry presents nineteenth-century geometry as a transformation in both mathematics and the philosophy of knowledge. Euclid’s fifth postulate had long been treated as necessary or self-evident, yet Lobachevsky and Bolyai developed geometry by rejecting it. In that setting, triangles have angle sums below two right angles, and familiar Euclidean results such as the existence of rectangles no longer hold. Projective geometry pursued properties stable under projection. To avoid failures caused by parallelism, it introduced ideal points and an ideal plane, producing a geometry whose ordering relations differ sharply from ordinary intuition. Klein’s Erlangen program sought unity amid this proliferation: a geometry is studied through a manifold, a group of transformations, and the features invariant under that group. His work connected projective structures with Euclidean, Lobachevskian, and elliptic metric geometries, while Poincaré used the group perspective to motivate a conventionalist view of geometry’s application to physics. The axiomatic movement, especially in Pasch and Hilbert, made deductive completeness explicit. Primitive terms need not retain ordinary meanings in every model; what matters formally is the network of relations imposed by the axioms. Riemann then proposed a more general differential geometry of continuous manifolds, using local metric structure and curvature. Constant-curvature spaces fit Klein’s classification, but variable-curvature Riemannian geometries show that the Erlangen framework is too narrow to encompass all geometry. Lie groups unite group operations with smooth manifolds and later became central to mathematical physics. key_ideas: The non-Euclidean revolution showed that Euclidean geometry is one member of a wider family, challenging claims that it uniquely expresses necessary knowledge of space.
Projective geometry enlarged the mathematical setting with ideal points and treated incidence properties through collineations, making its structure both powerful and counterintuitive.
Klein’s Erlangen program characterized a geometry by a space together with a transformation group and the invariants of that group.
Nineteenth-century axiomatics separated deduction from the meanings of primitive terms and from the evidence supplied by diagrams; models could reveal independence of axioms.
Riemann generalized geometry to continuous manifolds with local metric structure and variable curvature, a framework not fully captured by Klein’s group-theoretic classification.
Lie groups combined algebraic composition with smooth structure, supplying mathematical tools later used to organize physical theories.
summaries.why_it_matters: The nineteenth-century developments changed what counts as a geometric theory and weakened the idea that Euclidean geometry is automatically the necessary form of space. They distinguished formal deduction from visual intuition, mathematical possibility from empirical choice, and local geometric structure from global symmetry. These distinctions remain important when mathematics is used in science: a physical theory may select a geometry because of evidence, explanatory power, or structural fit rather than because that geometry is the only logically possible one.

important_terms.definition: A rule requested as a starting point for a geometric system; Euclid’s fifth concerns when lines meeting a transversal must meet one another.
A geometry developed from Euclidean assumptions except for the fifth postulate, whose negation is adopted; its triangles have angle sums below two right angles.
Geometry concerned with properties preserved by projection or, more formally, by suitable collineations.
A one-to-one transformation of a space onto itself that preserves the relevant structure; in Klein’s framework, groups of such transformations organize geometries.
A feature unchanged by every transformation in a specified group.
A formal foundation using basic terms, relations, and axioms from which conclusions are derived without relying on diagrams or intuitive meanings.
A geometry of a continuous space equipped with a way to measure lengths locally; its curvature may be constant or variable.
A group that is also a smooth manifold, with multiplication and inversion varying smoothly; rotations provide a basic example.

questions_to_think_about: If several geometries are mathematically legitimate, what determines which one describes physical space?
Does a model with unusual objects weaken an axiom system, or does it clarify what the axioms actually say?
Why can projective geometry preserve incidence while changing lengths and angles?
What is gained, and what may be lost, by classifying a geometry through its transformation group?
How does Riemannian geometry expose a limitation in the Erlangen program?

summaries.example: Suppose you draw a picture on a transparent sheet and shine a light through it onto another sheet. The picture may become larger or thinner, but lines that meet still meet at the projected meeting point. Projective geometry focuses on such preserved relationships, not on ordinary measurements like length. To handle a line that seems to disappear when it becomes parallel to the target sheet, projective geometry adds an ideal point representing that direction.
summaries.summary: The nineteenth century brought a major expansion of geometry. For a long time, people often thought Euclid’s geometry was the natural model of certainty. A central issue was Euclid’s fifth postulate, which describes how certain lines eventually meet. Lobachevsky and Bolyai explored what happens when this postulate is rejected. They developed a non-Euclidean geometry in which triangle angles add to less than two right angles and some ordinary shapes, such as rectangles, cannot exist. Projective geometry took a different path. It studied what stays the same when a figure is projected from one plane to another. Since parallel lines create awkward missing points, projective geometry added ideal points for directions. These points make the system more unified, although they also make its idea of order very unlike everyday geometry. Felix Klein tried to organize the many branches of geometry with the Erlangen program. He described a geometry using a space and a group of transformations. A group is a collection of changes that can be combined, undone, and treated as an identity change. The important features are the invariants: what remains unchanged under those transformations. The period also improved the axiomatic method. Pasch and Hilbert emphasized that proofs must use stated assumptions, not hidden facts suggested by a diagram. This meant that the basic words in a theory could be interpreted in different models as long as the required relations held. Riemann proposed an even broader approach to geometry, one that could describe curved spaces and changing curvature. Lie groups later combined smooth spaces with algebraic operations and became useful in physics. key_ideas: Euclid’s geometry was once treated as especially certain, but nineteenth-century mathematicians built other geometries by changing one postulate.
Lobachevskian geometry is not merely a mistake in drawing; it is a different system with its own surprising results.
Projective geometry studies relationships that survive projection and uses ideal points to make the theory more complete.
Klein’s Erlangen program said that a geometry can be understood through its transformations and the properties they preserve.
Pasch and Hilbert helped make proofs more rigorous by requiring every needed assumption to be stated.
Riemann’s geometry allowed curvature to vary, showing that Klein’s way of classifying geometries did not cover everything.
summaries.why_it_matters: The history of nineteenth-century geometry shows how questioning a familiar rule can lead to powerful new ideas. It also helps explain the difference between a mathematical choice and an empirical discovery. Mathematics can describe several possible structures, while experiments may help decide which structure best fits the physical world. Careful axioms then tell us exactly what follows from each choice.

important_terms.definition: A basic rule accepted at the beginning of a geometric theory, rather than proved from earlier geometric rules.
A statement shown to follow from definitions and accepted starting rules.
A geometry that results when Euclid’s fifth postulate is denied; triangle angles have a total smaller than two right angles.
The study of features of figures that remain unchanged under projection-like transformations.
A change that maps a space back onto itself, such as moving, rotating, or otherwise rearranging its points in a permitted way.
A feature that a chosen transformation does not change.
A careful system of basic terms and rules from which conclusions are proved step by step.
A general approach to curved or variable spaces that describes local distances and curvature.

questions_to_think_about: Should a geometric system be judged by familiar pictures, by logical consistency, or by usefulness in science?
Why might mathematicians add ideal points instead of treating parallel cases as annoying exceptions?
How can two theories use the same word, such as “point,” while giving it different roles?
What might experiments tell us that deduction alone cannot tell us about physical space?
Why is a geometry with changing curvature more general than one with constant curvature?
